title: Data Structures
description: The structures behind fast solutions: what each guarantees and when to reach for it.

entries.title: Arrays and Dynamic Arrays
entries.summary: Contiguous memory gives O(1) indexing and cache-friendly scans; appends amortize to O(1) by doubling. The default structure until access patterns say otherwise.
entries.how_it_works: Elements sit back-to-back, so address = base + i * size. Appends write past the end; when full, allocate double the capacity and copy. Copy cost spreads over the appends since the last doubling.

complexity.time: O(1) index/append amortized, O(n) insert/remove mid

entries.example:
# Python lists are dynamic arrays.
# Reserve when the size is known:
a = [0] * 1000          # O(n) once, avoids regrowth
# Prefer local append in loops:
app = a.append
for x in range(1000):
    app(x)
pitfalls: [[]] * n aliases the same inner list
Insert at index 0 is O(n) every time
Resizing inside a hot loop without reserving
tips: Preallocate when the final size is known
Use collections.deque for double-ended queues
array('i') or numpy for huge numeric buffers

entries.title: Linked Lists
entries.summary: Nodes chained by pointers give O(1) splice at known positions but O(n) access by index. Mostly a teaching tool and interview topic; arrays win in practice.
recognize: Constant-time insert/delete with an iterator in hand
Implementing stacks, queues, or LRU skeletons
entries.how_it_works: Each node stores data plus a next (and maybe prev) reference. Insert/delete rewires a constant number of links. Traversal follows links one hop at a time with no skipping.

complexity.time: O(1) splice at position, O(n) index/search

pitfalls: Losing the rest of the list by overwriting next too early
Dummy head forgotten on edge cases
Cycles from bad rewiring
tips: Dummy head node kills special cases
Draw boxes-and-arrows before coding
Reach for deque/array instead in real code

entries.title: Stacks
entries.summary: Last-in-first-out with push, pop, and peek. Recursion, undo, bracket matching, and monotonic scans are all stack applications.
entries.how_it_works: Push adds to the top, pop removes from it — both O(1) amortized on a dynamic array. The call stack is an implicit stack; making it explicit enables pausing, inspecting, or reordering work.
pitfalls: Popping an empty stack
Forgetting leftovers mean unbalanced
Recursion depth when the stack is implicit
tips: Store (value, index) pairs for span problems
Two stacks implement a queue
Min-stack keeps parallel minima

entries.title: Queues and Deques
entries.summary: First-in-first-out order for BFS layers, task scheduling, and sliding windows. A deque adds O(1) pushes and pops on both ends.
entries.how_it_works: Enqueue at the back, dequeue from the front. A ring buffer or linked chunks keep both ends O(1); collections.deque is the standard choice. Monotone deques additionally evict dominated elements.
pitfalls: list.pop(0) is O(n) — use deque
Stale indices not evicted from the window
<= vs < changes which equal element survives
tips: BFS frontier? Reach for deque immediately
Monotone deque solves sliding max/min in O(n)
Priority queue is a different tool (see ds.heap)

entries.title: Hash Maps and Sets
entries.summary: Average O(1) lookup, insert, and delete by hashing keys into buckets. The single highest-leverage structure for turning brute force into linear passes.
entries.how_it_works: A hash function maps each key to a bucket; collisions resolve by chaining or open addressing. Load factor triggers rehashing, keeping chains short on average. Iteration order is unspecified.
pitfalls: Worst-case blowup on adversarial keys
Mutating a key after inserting it
Assuming iteration order
tips: setdefault/defaultdict remove boilerplate
For tiny fixed domains, arrays beat dicts
Hash the canonical form (sorted tuple, frozenset)

entries.title: Heaps and Priority Queues
entries.summary: A binary heap serves the min (or max) in O(1) and inserts/extracts in O(log n). Scheduling, top-k, and Dijkstra all lean on it.
entries.how_it_works: A complete binary tree in array form where each parent beats its children. Insert bubbles up, extract moves the last element to the root and sifts down. heapq is a min-heap; negate keys for max behavior.
pitfalls: heapq has no decrease-key (push duplicates, skip stale)
Max-heap via negation breaks on tuples with ties
heapify is O(n), not O(n log n)
tips: Lazy deletion: skip stale entries on pop
Two heaps track running medians
Tuples need a unique tiebreaker after negation

entries.title: Binary Search Trees
entries.summary: Ordered structure with left < node < right invariant giving O(h) search, insert, delete, min, max, predecessor, successor. Degenerate input makes h = n without balancing.
recognize: Understanding what balanced trees improve on
entries.how_it_works: Search descends left or right by comparison. Insert lands at an empty child slot. Delete splices: leaf drops, single-child links through, two-children swaps with the successor then deletes it.
entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE search/insert/delete:
  search(node, x): node is None -> miss; x == node.key -> hit;
    else recurse into the smaller/larger side
  insert: descend to empty child, attach new node
  delete: 0/1 children splice through; 2 children swap with inorder successor, delete successor
pitfalls: Sorted input builds a stick (need self-balancing)
Successor-swap delete corrupts parent links if rushed
Duplicates policy must be consistent
tips: Inorder traversal yields sorted order — free validation
bisect on sorted arrays wins for static data
Real libraries use red-black/AVL underneath

entries.title: Tries
entries.summary: A tree of string prefixes sharing common beginnings, with end-markers for complete words. Prefix queries, autocomplete, and XOR-max problems follow.
entries.how_it_works: Each edge is a character; each node is a prefix. Insert walks/creates edges and marks the terminal. Search walks edges; missing edge means absent. Children live in arrays (small alphabet) or dicts.

complexity.time: O(L) per word op, L = length

pitfalls: Forgetting end markers (prefixes match as words)
Memory blowup on huge alphabets (compress or hash children)
Deleting words needs refcounting
tips: Bitwise trie solves max-XOR-pair
Aho-Corasick extends tries to multi-pattern search
Sort + binary search competes for static dictionaries

entries.title: Union-Find (DSU)
entries.summary: Maintain disjoint sets with near-constant union and find via path compression plus union by rank. Connectivity, Kruskal, and offline queries all use it.
recognize: Process queries offline in reverse (deletions become additions)
entries.how_it_works: Each set is a tree rooted at its representative. Find climbs with path compression (flatten on the way). Union attaches the shorter tree under the taller, keeping depth near the inverse Ackermann function.
pitfalls: No splitting: deletions need offline reversal
Forgetting compression (degrades to O(n))
1-based vs 0-based element ids
tips: Reverse-time trick converts deletions to unions
Track size for component-size queries
Bipartite DSU (parity) checks 2-colorability

entries.title: Segment Trees
entries.summary: A binary tree over array intervals answering range queries and point/range updates in O(log n). The general tool when Fenwick's prefix-only view is insufficient.
entries.how_it_works: Leaves hold elements; each parent merges children with an associative op. Queries visit O(log n) disjoint nodes covering the range. Lazy tags postpone range updates to visited nodes only.
entries.example:
# Iterative max segment tree (size = power of two):
def build(a):
    n = 1
    while n < len(a):
        n *= 2
    t = [float('-inf')] * (2 * n)
    t[n:n + len(a)] = a
    for i in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
        t[i] = max(t[2 * i], t[2 * i + 1])
    return t, n

def point_update(t, n, i, x):
    i += n
    t[i] = x
    i //= 2
    while i:
        t[i] = max(t[2 * i], t[2 * i + 1])
        i //= 2
pitfalls: Non-associative ops break merging
Lazy propagation forgotten on push
Mixing 0/1-based indexing between tree and array
tips: Iterative trees are shorter and faster to write
Fenwick wins for prefix sums; segment tree for the rest
Beats/merge-sort trees extend the pattern

entries.title: Fenwick Tree (BIT)
entries.summary: Prefix sums with point updates in O(log n) using only an array and bit tricks. Shorter than a segment tree wherever prefix structure suffices.
entries.how_it_works: Tree[i] stores the sum of lowbit(i) elements ending at i. Updates climb by adding lowbit; queries descend by subtracting it. 1-based indexing makes the bit math work.
pitfalls: 0-based indexing breaks lowbit math (use 1-based)
Range add needs two BITs or difference tricks
Only invertible ops (no range min)
tips: Range sum = sum(r) - sum(l-1)
Binary lifting on the tree finds k-th one
Inversion count: sweep right to left summing smaller seen

entries.title: Sparse Table
entries.summary: Precompute interval answers for all power-of-two lengths to answer idempotent range queries (min, max, gcd, AND) in O(1). Static data only.
entries.how_it_works: st[k][i] answers length-2^k starting at i, built by halving. A query [l, r] takes k = floor(log2(len)) and combines the two overlapping blocks [l, l+2^k) and (r-2^k, r]; overlap is harmless for idempotent ops.

complexity.time: O(n log n) build, O(1) query

entries.example:
import math
def build(a, op):
    n = len(a)
    K = n.bit_length()
    st = [a[:]]
    j = 1
    while (1 << j) <= n:
        prev, step = st[-1], 1 << (j - 1)
        st.append([op(prev[i], prev[i + step]) for i in range(n - (1 << j) + 1)])
        j += 1
    logs = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        logs[i] = logs[i // 2] + 1
    return st, logs

def query(st, logs, op, l, r):  # inclusive
    k = logs[r - l + 1]
    return op(st[k][l], st[k][r - (1 << k) + 1])
pitfalls: Only idempotent ops (sum needs disjoint partition)
Log table off-by-one
Memory: n log n integers
tips: LCA in O(1): Euler tour depths + RMQ min
Faster queries than segment trees, zero updates
Precompute logs once, reuse

entries.title: Square Root Decomposition
entries.summary: Split the array into blocks of size ~sqrt(n); answer queries by combining whole blocks with brute-forced edges. Simple Mo's-algorithm foundation with update support.
recognize: Range queries with point updates, moderate constraints
entries.how_it_works: Precompute each block's aggregate. Queries scan at most two partial blocks element-wise and O(#blocks) whole blocks. Updates refresh one element and its block aggregate. Block size ~sqrt(n) balances both costs.
entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE range sum with point updates, block size B:
  blocks[b] = sum of a[b*B : (b+1)*B]
  update(i, x): a[i] = x; rebuild block i//B
  query(l, r):
    ans = 0
    while l <= r and l % B: ans += a[l]; l += 1      # left edge
    while l + B - 1 <= r: ans += blocks[l//B]; l += B  # whole blocks
    while l <= r: ans += a[l]; l += 1                  # right edge
    return ans
pitfalls: Wrong block size (tune to operation costs)
Edge loops with inclusive/exclusive confusion
Lazy per-block state needs care
tips: Mo's algorithm = sqrt-decomp over queries
Block size n^(2/3) with updates (Mo's with modifications)
Prototype here before reaching for fancier trees

entries.title: Suffix Automaton (SAM)
entries.summary: A minimal automaton of all substrings built online in linear time: each extension clones at most one state. Substring queries, distinct-substring counts, and LCS follow.
entries.how_it_works: Extend character by character: create a cur state, walk suffix links adding missing transitions, clone the state where the path diverges. Clone copies transitions with a smaller maxlen. Occurrence counts propagate in length order.
entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE extend(c):
  cur = new state(len = last.len + 1)
  p = last
  while p exists and c not in p.next: p.next[c] = cur; p = p.link
  if no such p: cur.link = root
  else:
    q = p.next[c]
    if p.len + 1 == q.len: cur.link = q
    else: clone q (copy next, link; len = p.len + 1); redirect transitions; cur.link = q.link = clone
  last = cur
pitfalls: Clone must copy transitions AND link, with len = p.len+1
Counting occurrences needs end-pos propagation
Multiple strings need separators or resets
tips: States <= 2n-1 bounds memory
Distinct substrings = sum(len[v] - len[link[v]])
Suffix array/trie is simpler for offline queries

entries.title: Treap (Randomized BST)
entries.summary: A BST by key and heap by random priority: rotations maintain both, giving expected logarithmic operations with short code. Split/merge make sequence treaps (implicit keys) easy.
entries.how_it_works: Random priorities make the shape a random BST (expected log height). Split by key into (<k, >=k); merge assumes all keys of one precede the other, recursing on the higher-priority root. Implicit variant splits by subtree size.
pitfalls: Forgetting update() (sizes/sums) after rewiring
Priority collisions (use wide random range)
Recursion depth on adversarial splits (unlikely but possible)
tips: Implicit treap: split by size for sequence ops
Lazy tags compose like segment trees
Splay is the amortized alternative

entries.title: Persistent Segment Tree
entries.summary: Path-copying on updates creates a new version sharing unchanged nodes: O(log n) new nodes per update. Versioned queries like k-th in a prefix become possible.
entries.how_it_works: Update clones nodes along the path, reusing other children pointers. roots[v] addresses version v. Querying two versions together (e.g. prefix r minus prefix l-1) walks both in lockstep for k-th order statistics.

complexity.space: O((n + q) log n) nodes total

entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE point update creating version new from old:
  update(node, l, r, i, v):
    new = clone(node)
    if l == r: new.sum += v; return new
    mid = (l + r) // 2
    if i <= mid: new.left = update(node.left, l, mid, i, v)
    else: new.right = update(node.right, mid+1, r, i, v)
    new.sum = new.left.sum + new.right.sum
    return new
pitfalls: Cloning before recursing (else old version mutates)
Node pool exhaustion (preallocate generously)
Summing versions requires aligned structure
tips: Chairman tree = persistent segtree for k-th queries
Merge-sort tree is the simpler static alternative
Functional style prevents aliasing bugs
